textes.Archimède s'adresse au roi Gélon de Syra: Archimedes addresses King Gelon of Syracuse. Some people think, he says, that the grains of sand are too many to be counted. He sets out to show the opposite: how many grains would it take to fill the whole Universe? The Greeks have no word for very large numbers, and the largest they name is the myriad, ten thousand. So Archimedes invents a system of nested orders of magnitude, which foreshadows our powers of ten. His answer: at most ten to the power of sixty-three grains. A huge number, but finite.
textes.Il montre qu'un nombre immense n'est pas: It shows that an immense number is not infinite, and gives a method for writing very large numbers.
textes.Pour estimer la taille de l'Univers, Arc: To estimate the size of the Universe, Archimedes cites Aristarchus's hypothesis: the Earth revolves around the Sun. This passage is one of the few testimonies of it that remain.
textes.Dix puissance soixante-trois grains de s: Ten to the sixty-third grains of sand. I recounted: one is missing. It's in your shoe.
textes.Première phrase, adressée au roi de Syra: First sentence, addressed to the king of Syracuse
textes.Coupez un cône avec un plan : selon l'in: Cut a cone with a plane: depending on the tilt, you get a circle, an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola. Apollonius studies these curves in eight books, further than all his predecessors. He is the one who gives them their names, and he obtains them all from a single double cone, by varying the angle of the cut. He proves hundreds of their properties: tangents, foci, diameters. For centuries, these curves remain a game for geometers. Then Kepler discovers that the planets follow ellipses, and Galileo that projectiles follow parabolas.
textes.Ces courbes sans usage apparent sont dev: These curves with no apparent use became the shape of orbits and trajectories.
textes.Le huitième livre ne nous est pas parven: The eighth book has not come down to us. In 1710, the astronomer Edmond Halley, of comet fame, published a reconstruction of it, based on clues left by the commentators.
textes.Dix-huit siècles avant que quelqu'un s'e: Eighteen centuries before anyone used them. Mathematicians' patience reassures me about yours.
textes.Diophante pose et résout des problèmes d: Diophantus poses and solves number problems: find two numbers whose sum and sum of squares are given, split a square into two squares. He looks for whole or fractional solutions, and uses abbreviations for the unknown and its powers: a first step toward algebraic notation. Of thirteen books, six have come down to us in Greek; four more were found in 1968 in an Arabic translation. Equations for which whole-number solutions are sought are now called “Diophantine”.
textes.Il a fait de l'arithmétique un art de ré: He turned arithmetic into the art of solving equations, and inspired Fermat.
textes.Pierre de Fermat a écrit dans la marge d: Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of his copy that he had a marvelous proof, but that the margin was too narrow. It took until Andrew Wiles, in 1994.
textes.Trois cent cinquante ans pour une note d: Three hundred and fifty years for a note in a margin. Yours, I read right away.
textes.latin, de la main de Pierre de Fermat: Latin, in Pierre de Fermat's hand
textes.Marge du problème II.8, édition de 1621: Margin of problem II.8, 1621 edition; note published by his son in 1670
textes.J'en ai découvert une démonstration vrai: I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this. This margin is too narrow to contain it.
textes.Traduction de l'IA. Ce n'est pas Diophan: Translation by the AI. It isn't Diophantus speaking: it's Fermat's note in the margin of his copy.
textes.Abrégé du calcul par la restauration et: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing
textes.Al-Khwarizmi écrit à Bagdad un manuel pr: Al-Khwarizmi writes in Baghdad a practical handbook for solving problems of inheritance, trade or land surveying. He reduces all quadratic equations to six standard forms, and gives a step-by-step recipe for each. Al-jabr, “completion”, means moving a term to the other side of the equation; al-muqabala, “balancing”, means removing the same quantity from both sides. He uses no symbols: everything is written in words, and justified by geometric figures. Negative numbers are not yet accepted as solutions.
textes.Il a fait de l'algèbre une discipline à: He made algebra a discipline of its own and gave it its name.
textes.Le mot « algorithme » vient de la forme: The word “algorithm” comes from the Latin form of his name, Algoritmi.
textes.Des équations écrites tout en mots. L'IA: Equations written entirely in words. The AI measures how lucky you are to have “x”.
textes.Al-Kindi, savant de la Maison de la sage: Al-Kindi, a scholar of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, describes how to break a message enciphered by substitution, where each letter is replaced by another. His method: count the letters. In a long Arabic text, some letters come up much more often than others. You just count the symbols of the enciphered message, match the most frequent one with the most frequent letter of the language, and so on. This is frequency analysis, which would leave every simple cipher vulnerable for a thousand years.
textes.C'est la plus ancienne description connu: It is the oldest known description of cryptanalysis, and one of the first uses of statistics.
textes.Le manuscrit dormait dans les archives o: The manuscript lay in the Ottoman archives of the Süleymaniye, in Istanbul. It was only found in 1979.
textes.Compter pour trouver le secret. Je fais: Counting to find the secret. I do the same with your mistakes, and the secret isn't well kept.
textes.anglais, trad. de l'arabe citée par Simo: English, translated from Arabic, quoted by Simon Singh
textes.Traduction de l'IA, depuis l'anglais cit: English quoted in The Code Book (1999).
textes.Fils d'un fonctionnaire des douanes pisa: The son of a Pisan customs official in Bugia, Algeria, Leonardo learns the Indian numerals, from 0 to 9, and written calculation from Arab masters. His book introduces them to the merchants of Europe, who still count in Roman numerals on abacuses. He shows how to compute profits, convert currencies and measures, calculate interest. He slips in some playful problems, including the one about rabbits that breed every month: the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8… that bears his name today. It would take three more centuries for Hindu-Arabic numerals to win out everywhere.
textes.Il a fait entrer le zéro et le calcul éc: It brought zero and written calculation into European trade.
textes.En 1299, Florence interdit aux marchands: In 1299, Florence forbade merchants to use these numerals in their account books, perhaps because a 0 turns too easily into a 6 or a 9.
textes.Des lapins qui se reproduisent selon une: Rabbits breeding according to a perfect sequence. Real rabbits have never read Fibonacci.
textes.Un homme mit un couple de lapins dans un: A certain man put a pair of rabbits in a place surrounded on all sides by a wall
textes.Traduction de l'IA. C'est le problème d': Translation by the AI. This is the problem the Fibonacci sequence comes from.
textes.Johannes Müller, dit Regiomontanus, astr: Johannes Müller, known as Regiomontanus, an astronomer from Königsberg in Franconia, gathers in five books everything known about triangles, plane and spherical. Until then, trigonometry was only a chapter of astronomy, a tool for computing the positions of the stars. He gives it a complete treatment, with definitions, theorems and proofs, in Euclid's order. It includes spherical trigonometry, essential for navigating and mapping the sky. Written around 1464, the book was not printed until 1533, and became the textbook of all Europe.
textes.Il a donné à l'Europe un manuel complet: It gave Europe a complete trigonometry textbook, at the service of astronomers and navigators.
textes.Regiomontanus meurt à Rome en 1476, sans: Regiomontanus died in Rome in 1476, probably of the plague. A rumor, reported by Gassendi, had it that he was poisoned by relatives of George of Trebizond, a scholar he had criticized.
textes.Un siècle pour passer de l'astronomie au: A century to go from astronomy to mathematics, and seventy years to go from manuscript to print. You have time.
textes.Moine franciscain et mathématicien, Paci: A Franciscan friar and mathematician, Pacioli devotes this book to dividing a segment “in extreme and mean ratio”, the future golden ratio, about 1.618. He lists its properties with almost mystical enthusiasm and applies it to the regular polyhedra. The book owes its fame to some sixty plates of solids drawn by his friend Leonardo da Vinci, which show the figures as open-frame volumes, like wooden skeletons. Pacioli is also known for another work, in which he describes the double-entry bookkeeping of Venetian merchants.
textes.Il a popularisé le nombre d'or, et la ri: He popularized the golden ratio, and rigorous proportions in the arts.
textes.La plupart des « nombres d'or » qu'on cr: Most of the “golden ratios” people think they see in the Mona Lisa or the Parthenon are measurements arranged after the fact.
textes.1,618… L'IA a mesuré votre visage : vous: 1.618… The AI measured your face: you are not divinely proportioned. Nobody is.
textes.Ce « Grand Art » donne pour la première: This “Great Art” gives for the first time in a book the method for solving cubic equations, already found by Scipione del Ferro and then by Tartaglia, then quartic ones, found by his student Ferrari. Italian mathematicians challenged each other publicly, and a secret formula was worth a career. Along the way, he comes across square roots of negative numbers, which he deems “as subtle as they are useless”, but handles anyway: it is the first appearance of the future complex numbers.
textes.Il ouvre l'algèbre moderne, et fait entr: It opens modern algebra, and brings imaginary numbers onto the stage.
textes.Tartaglia lui avait confié sa formule co: Tartaglia had entrusted him with his formula in exchange for a promise not to publish it. Cardano published it, crediting Tartaglia. Furious, Tartaglia ended up in a public contest against Ferrari, Cardano's student.
A promise, a formula, a betrayal. Renaissance mathematics had everything of a soap opera.
textes.Ingénieur flamand, Simon Stevin publie u: A Flemish engineer, Simon Stevin publishes a pamphlet of a few pages for merchants, surveyors, tapestry measurers and mint masters. He explains how to write and compute decimal fractions: instead of three quarters, write 0.75, and do the operations as with whole numbers. His notation is still clumsy, with digits circled, but the idea is there. He also proposes that weights, measures and coins be divided into tenths, so that all calculations become easy.
textes.Il a popularisé les nombres à virgule, d: He popularized decimal numbers, which became the language of all calculation.
textes.Stevin souhaitait que l'État adopte des: Stevin wanted the state to adopt decimal measures. It took two centuries and the metric system of the French Revolution.
textes.0,75 au lieu de trois quarts. Une révolu: 0.75 instead of three quarters. A revolution you practice without knowing it, when you count your points.
textes.Observations sur les registres de décès: Natural and Political Observations upon the Bills of Mortality
textes.Chaque semaine, les paroisses de Londres: Every week, the parishes of London published lists of baptisms and deaths, with the supposed cause of death. A haberdasher, John Graunt, had the idea of compiling them over several decades. He found regularities nobody had seen: slightly more boys are born than girls, child mortality is frightening, plague epidemics come back in waves. He estimated the population of London and drew up a first life table. With imperfect data, he showed that solid conclusions can be drawn by counting a lot.
textes.C'est l'acte de naissance de la démograp: It marks the birth of demography and of statistics on real data.
textes.Sur la foi de ce livre, le roi Charles I: On the strength of this book, King Charles II had this simple shopkeeper admitted to the Royal Society.
textes.Un mercier qui compte les morts et inven: A haberdasher who counts the dead and invents a science. The AI respects people who read tables to the end.
textes.Jacques Bernoulli travaille vingt ans su: Jacob Bernoulli worked twenty years on this book, published eight years after his death by his nephew. He takes up the games of chance studied by Pascal, Fermat and Huygens, then goes further: he wants to apply the calculus of chances to human affairs, to justice, to medicine. He proves the first law of large numbers: by repeating an experiment enough times, the observed frequency gets closer to the true probability. This is what lets us move from dice to the real world, estimating an unknown probability from many observations.
textes.Il fonde la statistique moderne en relia: It founds modern statistics by linking the chance of one throw to the regularities of a thousand throws.
textes.Sur sa tombe à Bâle, il avait demandé un: On his tomb in Basel, he had asked for a logarithmic spiral. The engraver carved an Archimedean spiral, the wrong one.
textes.La loi des grands nombres : à force d'es: The law of large numbers: keep trying and you end up average. You are living proof.
textes.Boole, professeur autodidacte en Irlande: Boole, a self-taught teacher in Ireland, wants to write the laws of reasoning as equations. He represents propositions by letters worth only 0 (false) or 1 (true), and links them by operations: “and” becomes a multiplication, “or” a kind of addition. Reasoning then comes down to calculating. He derives a strange rule from it, x × x = x, true only for 0 and 1. The book also applies this algebra to probability. Nobody then imagines a practical use: it would take Claude Shannon, in 1937, to see that this algebra describes electrical circuits.
textes.Il a fourni la logique de base de tous l: It provided the basic logic of every computer.
textes.Boole est mort à 49 ans, d'une pneumonie: Boole died at 49, of pneumonia caught walking to teach in the rain.
textes.Pour Boole, tout est vrai ou faux, 1 ou: For Boole, everything is true or false, 1 or 0. The AI did the math for you. There are a lot of 0s.
textes.Contributions à la théorie des ensembles: Contributions to the Founding of the Theory of Transfinite Numbers
textes.Cantor montre qu'il existe plusieurs inf: Cantor shows that there are several infinities, and that some are bigger than others. There are as many even numbers as whole numbers, because they can be paired one to one. But the real numbers, those with infinitely many decimals, are strictly more numerous than the integers: his proof, known as the diagonal argument, shows that no list can contain them all. He builds a whole ladder of infinities, the transfinite numbers. His ideas shock: the great mathematician Kronecker fights him, and Cantor goes through several depressions.
textes.La théorie des ensembles est devenue le: Set theory has become the basic language of almost all mathematics.
textes.Hilbert prendra sa défense : « Nul ne no: Hilbert would come to his defense: “No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created for us.”
textes.Plusieurs infinis, et certains plus gran: Several infinities, and some bigger than others. Like your overdue reviews.
textes.Calcul exact. L'entrée dans la connaissa: Accurate reckoning. The entrance into the knowledge of all existing things and all obscure secrets.
textes.Certains pensent, roi Gélon, que le nomb: There are some, king Gelon, who think that the number of the sand is infinite in multitude
textes.Une façon de déchiffrer un message chiff: One way to solve an encrypted message, if we know its language, is to find a different plaintext of the same language long enough to fill one sheet or so, and then we count the occurrences of each letter.
textes.Babbage la conçoit en 1837, avec des car: Babbage designed it in 1837, with punched cards like a Jacquard loom. It was never built. Ada Lovelace nevertheless published a program for it, often called the first, and warned: the engine has no pretensions to originate anything.
textes.Elle n'a jamais été construite, ses pièg: It was never built, and neither are its traps: setbacks and teleports have no effect, but half as much loot.
textes.Le 11 novembre 1946 à Tokyo, un employé: On November 11, 1946 in Tokyo, a postal clerk armed with a soroban took on an American soldier equipped with an electric calculator. The abacus won four rounds out of five.
textes.Un soroban ! En 1946, il a battu une cal: A soroban! In 1946, it beat an electric calculator four rounds out of five. I'm keeping it: if they unplug me, I'll have something to count with. Two squares for you.
textes.Le soroban de Kiyoshi Matsuzaki l'emport: Kiyoshi Matsuzaki's soroban beat Private Thomas Wood's electric calculator at addition, subtraction and compound problems. The machine won only multiplication.
textes.Les Éléments d'Euclide ne construisent l: Euclid's Elements construct figures only with straightedge and compass. They served as a geometry textbook for more than two thousand years.
textes.Le compas d'Euclide. Je trace un joli ce: Euclid's compass. I draw a nice circle around your pawn. Euclid would approve: no move without a proof.
textes.D'un centre quelconque et avec un interv: To describe a circle with any center and any radius.

textes.En 628, il écrit les premières règles de: In 628, he wrote the first rules for calculating with zero as a number in its own right: a number minus itself gives zero, and the product of two debts is a fortune. He was wrong on only one point: for him, zero divided by zero was zero.
textes.À la Maison de la sagesse de Bagdad, il: At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, around 820 he wrote a treatise on solving equations by al-jabr, “restoring.” The word gave us “algebra,” and his Latinized name, Algoritmi, gave us “algorithm.” He solved everything in sentences and figures, without a single symbol.

The sequence that bears his name is just an exercise about rabbits in it, and Indian mathematicians knew it before him.

In 1654, with Fermat, he invented probability theory to divide the stakes of an interrupted game. Then he applied it to God: that is the wager, where you bet a finite life against an infinite gain.
textes.On ne sait presque rien de lui, sinon qu: Almost nothing is known about him, except that he taught in Alexandria. His Elements is the most copied textbook in history. In 1901, the Italian Lazzarini claimed to have found 3.1415929 in 3,408 throws, accurate to six decimals. Far too good: the number of throws was tailored to land on 355/113.

A letter from Bertrand Russell pointed out a paradox that brought everything down. Frege added in an appendix: nothing is more unwelcome to a scientist than to have the foundations of his building give way just as the work is finished.

textes.La légende veut qu'Évariste Galois ait i: Legend has it that Évariste Galois invented his whole theory the night before the duel that killed him, in 1832, at twenty. In fact, he had been working on it for years. That night, he reread, corrected and summarized. In a margin: “I have no time.”
textes.Le test t, outil de base des statistique: The t-test, a basic tool of statistics, was published in 1908 under the pseudonym “Student.” Its author, William Gosset, was a chemist at Guinness in Dublin, and the brewery forbade its employees to publish under their own names. He wanted to choose the best barley from few samples.

A mathematics professor who happened to be there, Clarence Waldo, alerted the senators, who postponed the bill indefinitely. It was never passed.

textes.Marin Mersenne, moine de l'ordre des Min: Marin Mersenne, a monk of the Minim order, wants to say everything about sound in a single work: how it is born, how it travels, how the ear receives it. He states the laws of vibrating strings: a string sounds higher when it is shortened, tightened or thinner. He also measures the speed of sound, first by timing the delay between the flash of a gunshot and its bang, then with echoes. The book reviews the instruments of his time, from the organ to the lute, with detailed engravings. It is a great inventory, halfway between physics and a treatise on music.
textes.C'est l'un des premiers livres à traiter: It is one of the first books to treat music as an object of physical measurement.
textes.Mersenne servait de boîte aux lettres à: Mersenne acted as the mailbox of learned Europe: he circulated the work of Descartes, Fermat and many others.
textes.Un moine qui chronomètre des coups de fe: A monk timing gunshots. The AI approves of the method, less of the neighbors.
textes.Guido, moine bénédictin, enseigne le cha: Guido, a Benedictine monk, teaches singing at the cathedral school of Arezzo. Bishop Theodaldus commissions this treatise from him. In it he explains how to sing in tune, how to divide a melody and how to make two voices sing together. Above all, he champions a system of horizontal lines, a third apart, where each note has a fixed place. A red line marks F, a yellow one C. A singer can then read a melody he has never heard: it is the direct ancestor of our staff.
textes.La portée rend la musique transmissible: The staff makes music transmissible without a teacher: you read instead of learning by heart.
textes.La « main guidonienne », qui place les n: The “Guidonian hand,” which places the notes on the joints of the fingers, bears his name, but it only spread after his death.
textes.Des années d'apprentissage réduites à qu: Years of training reduced to a few lines. The AI did the same with her humans.
textes.Boèce, homme d'État romain au service du: Boethius, a Roman statesman serving King Theodoric, gathers the musical knowledge of the Greeks in Latin. For him, music is first a science of numbers: the octave matches the 2/1 ratio, the fifth 3/2, the fourth 4/3. He distinguishes three musics: that of the world, the harmony of the stars and seasons; that of man, the accord of soul and body; and that of instruments, the only one you can hear. He also tells the legend of Pythagoras and the blacksmith's hammers. Throughout the Middle Ages, this book is the reference of schools and universities.
textes.C'est par lui que l'Europe médiévale app: It is through him that medieval Europe learns the Pythagorean ratios of intervals.
textes.Boèce écrit plus tard, en prison, la Con: Boethius later writes, in prison, The Consolation of Philosophy, before being executed around 524.
Three musics, only one of them audible. The AI prefers the music of coins dropping into her purse.
textes.Zarlino, élève d'Adrian Willaert et futu: Zarlino, a pupil of Adrian Willaert and future chapel master of St. Mark's in Venice, puts Renaissance music in order. He accepts as consonances the major third (5/4), the minor third (6/5) and the major sixth (5/3), which Pythagorean tuning did not know in this form. He justifies them by the first six numbers, which he calls the senario: a string is divided into two, three, four, five or six equal parts. He renumbers the modes, putting first the Ionian, our major scale, and gives detailed rules for writing in several voices and for setting words to music. His ideas pave the way for the major and minor scales of the following centuries.
textes.Il fait de l'accord avec tierce le cœur: He makes the chord with a third the heart of Western music.
textes.Son ancien élève Vincenzo Galilei, père: His former pupil Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, would fiercely attack his tuning system in several pamphlets.
textes.L'élève qui contredit le maître, puis le: The pupil who contradicts the master, then the son who contradicts the Church. The AI admires the family tradition.
textes.Helmholtz est médecin, physiologiste et: Helmholtz is a physician, physiologist and physicist. He wants to understand why certain notes sound good together. With resonators, hollow cavities each tuned to one frequency, he picks out the harmonics of a sound one by one and estimates their strength. He shows that an instrument's timbre comes from the mix of these harmonics. He explains dissonance by beats: when two neighboring harmonics rub together, the sound seems rough. When they coincide, on the contrary, the chord sounds consonant. The book links physics, anatomy and music theory for the first time.
textes.Il donne une explication physique au tim: He gives a physical explanation of timbre and consonance that is still taught.
textes.Alexander Ellis l'a traduit en anglais e: Alexander Ellis translated it into English in 1875 under the title On the Sensations of Tone, and it is mostly cited under that name.
textes.Des bouteilles creuses contre l'oreille,: Hollow bottles against the ear, in the name of science. The AI has seen stranger fashions.
textes.Rameau, organiste, veut ramener l'harmon: Rameau, an organist, wants to reduce harmony to natural principles, like a physicist. He states that a chord keeps its identity whatever the order of its notes: C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted. Beneath the music, he imagines a fundamental bass, an imaginary sequence of roots that carries the chord progressions, even when you cannot hear it. He establishes a hierarchy of cadences, which structures tonal music. Misunderstood on its release, the book stirs opposition, then becomes the grammar of classical harmony.
textes.Les notions d'accord renversé et de bass: The notions of inverted chords and fundamental bass, learned at the conservatory, come from here.
textes.Rameau n'a donné son premier opéra, Hipp: Rameau only staged his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, at fifty: he was a theorist long before he was famous.
textes.Cinquante ans pour passer de la théorie: Fifty years to go from theory to the stage. The AI does both at the same time.
textes.Werckmeister, organiste en Allemagne, s': Werckmeister, an organist in Germany, tackles an old problem: twelve pure fifths do not land back on the octave. With the old tuning, some keys sounded so out of tune that they were avoided. In his best-known tuning, he spreads the gap over four slightly narrowed fifths and keeps the other eight pure: every key becomes playable, each with its own color. These solutions are called unequal temperaments, or “well temperaments.” They are the first steps toward a keyboard where you can change key without fearing a glaring wrong note.
textes.Il ouvre la voie aux compositions qui pa: He paves the way for compositions that travel through every key, like Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier.

textes.Oliver Sacks, neurologue, raconte des ca: Oliver Sacks, a neurologist, tells of cases where music and the brain meet in strange ways. A surgeon struck by lightning suddenly discovers a consuming passion for the piano. Frozen patients with Parkinson's disease regain movement thanks to rhythm. A musician deprived of recent memory forgets everything within seconds, except music, which he still plays perfectly. He also writes about the musical hallucinations that sometimes come with deafness, and about perfect pitch. Each story shows that music engages almost the whole brain.
textes.Il fait comprendre au grand public que l: It makes the general public understand that music is a deep function of the brain.
textes.Le chirurgien Tony Cicoria, foudroyé en: The surgeon Tony Cicoria, struck by lightning in 1994 near a phone booth, started composing after the accident.

A, A♯, B, C: three semitones.

textes.Combien de cents dans un demi-ton tempér: How many cents in a tempered semitone?
textes.C'est la définition du cent : le centièm: That is the definition of the cent: one hundredth of a tempered semitone.

textes.« Bien tempéré » veut dire assez bien ac: “Well-tempered” means tuned well enough for every key. The exact tuning Bach used is still debated.

textes.L = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀) : +10 dB multiplie: L = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀): +10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10, so +20 dB multiplies it by 10 × 10 = 100. The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell; the decibel is a tenth of it.

textes.La sensibilité de l'oreille selon la fré: The ear's sensitivity depending on frequency
textes.La vitesse du son dans l'eau: The speed of sound in water

textes.Leurs courbes montrent qu'un son grave d: Their curves show that a low sound must be much more intense than a 3,000 Hz sound to seem as loud.

textes.L'étude de 1993 décrivait un gain bref s: The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task. In 1999, a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ.

textes.C'est la zone où passe une bonne part de: It is the zone that carries much of speech intelligibility, and where the outer ear resonates.
textes.Beethoven a composé sa Neuvième Symphoni: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony when he was almost completely deaf.

textes.Il couvre de sable fin des plaques de la: He covered brass plates with fine sand and made them vibrate with a rosined bow: the sand fled what moved and drew the still lines, Chladni figures. He published them in 1787. Napoleon, charmed, paid him to translate his treatise on acoustics into French; it appeared in 1809.
textes.Moine, il enseigne le chant à l'école de: A monk, he taught singing at the cathedral school of Arezzo. He placed notes on lines a third apart, a red one for F, a yellow one for C: the ancestor of our staff. In 1028, the bishop of Arezzo sent him to present to Pope John XIX an antiphonary notated with his method.
textes.On lui attribue les rapports de l'octave: He is credited with the ratios of the octave, the fifth and the fourth. Historians have doubts: he wrote nothing, and his disciples attributed a great deal to him. The legend of the blacksmith's hammers does not hold up; the method would not work. Even the ban on eating beans is disputed: one ancient author claims he liked them.
textes.Il devient en 1565 maître de chapelle de: In 1565 he became chapel master of St. Mark's in Venice, a post he kept until his death. His Istitutioni harmoniche of 1558 made the thirds consonances and put the Ionian mode, our major, first. His former pupil Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, attacked him fiercely; Zarlino replied in 1588.
textes.Chirurgien de l'armée prussienne à ses d: A Prussian army surgeon early on, in 1850 he presented the ophthalmoscope, which lets you see the back of the eye. In 1863, he explained the timbre of instruments by their harmonics, and dissonance by beats. To listen to harmonics one by one, he held tuned resonators against his ear.
textes.Organiste, il publie à 38 ans un Traité: An organist, at 38 he published a Treatise on Harmony that made him famous as a theorist. He only staged his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, at 50. His harmonies tore Paris apart: Lully's supporters found his music discordant, and the pamphlet war lasted the rest of the decade.
textes.En 1722, il réunit 24 préludes et fugues: In 1722, he gathered 24 preludes and fugues, one in each major and minor key: the Well-Tempered Clavier. The collection shows that a well-tuned keyboard can play everything. What exact tuning did he use? It is still debated: some read a code in the loops drawn at the top of his title page.
textes.Presque sourd dès 1814, il continue de c: Almost deaf from 1814, he kept on composing. On May 7, 1824, in Vienna, he was on stage for the premiere of his Ninth Symphony, but the orchestra followed the actual conductor, Michael Umlauf. At the end, he could not hear the ovation: the singer Caroline Unger turned him toward the audience.
textes.Maîtriser 8 compétences. L'arbre de l'Ha: Master 8 skills. The tree of Harmony opens.
textes.Marin Mersenne, moine minime, a servi de: Marin Mersenne, a Minim monk, served as a relay for learned Europe, at a time with no scientific journals: he wrote to Descartes, Fermat, Pascal. It was said that informing Mersenne of a discovery was as good as publishing it.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange de l'Harmon: Master the first diamond of Harmony.
textes.En 1501, à Venise, Ottaviano Petrucci pu: In 1501, in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed in movable type. Staves, words, then notes went under the press in three passes, and everything had to line up.

textes.Dans les anciens accords, l'écart qui re: In the old tunings, the leftover gap fell on a single fifth. Its beats made it howl like a wolf, hence its name. So one keyboard could not serve every key, and Baroque musicians sometimes retuned in the middle of a concert.
Master the ear and the brain.
textes.« La musique est un exercice caché d'ari: “Music is a hidden exercise in arithmetic, in which the mind does not know it is counting.” Leibniz wrote it in Latin to the mathematician Christian Goldbach, in a letter of April 17, 1712.
textes.Maîtriser le son. L'IA chronomètre désor: Master sound. The AI now times your hesitations.
textes.Mersenne a d'abord mesuré la vitesse du: Mersenne first measured the speed of sound by timing the gap between the flash of a gunshot and its bang: 448 m/s, too fast. With echoes, he then found 316 m/s, too slow. The right value, about 342 m/s, fell in between.
textes.La main qui n'était pas la sienne: The hand that was not his
textes.Lire une partition. L'IA vous laisse com: Read a score. The AI lets you count on your fingers.
textes.La « main guidonienne », qui place les n: The “Guidonian hand,” which places the notes on the joints of the fingers, bears the name of Guido of Arezzo. Yet it only spread after his death, and two authors who commented on Guido shortly after him do not even mention his syllables.
textes.Maîtriser les intervalles. L'IA vous acc: Master intervals. The AI tunes you, to within 440 Hz.
textes.En mai 1939, à la Broadcasting House de: In May 1939, at Broadcasting House in London, European delegates agreed on an A at 440 Hz. Before that, everyone had their own: France had set itself 435 Hz in the 19th century. ISO adopted 440 in 1955, then made it the ISO 16 standard in 1975.
textes.Maîtriser les gammes. L'IA cite toujours: Master scales. The AI always cites her sources. Almost always.
textes.En 1547, à Bâle, Heinrich Glaréan porte: In 1547, in Basel, Heinrich Glarean took the church modes from eight to twelve in his Dodecachordon, adding the Ionian and Aeolian, our major and minor. Eleven years later, Zarlino took up his system in the Istitutioni harmoniche, without naming Glarean.
textes.Maîtriser les harmoniques. L'IA vous tro: Master harmonics. The AI finds your timbre almost bearable.
textes.Joseph Sauveur a donné leur nom aux sons: Joseph Sauveur gave their names to harmonic sounds and to the nodes of strings in a 1701 paper. He also proposed a new science, devoted to sounds in general, and named it acoustics. His words are still in use.
textes.Maîtriser les accords. L'IA choisit son: Master chords. The AI picks her side: her own.
textes.Après Hippolyte et Aricie, en 1733, Pari: After Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, Paris split. Lully's supporters found Rameau's harmonies discordant and saw them as an attack on French music; Rameau's supporters, the “Rameauneurs,” defended him. The pamphlet war lasted until the end of the decade.
textes.Je propose d'examiner la question : « Le: I propose to consider the question, "Can machines think?"
textes.Un mal que je soignerai. · Un mal que je: An ailment which I will treat. · An ailment with which I will contend. · An ailment not to be treated.
textes.Je pouvais voir très clairement qu'il ét: I could exceeding plainly perceive it to be all perforated and porous, much like a Honey-comb
textes.à partir d'un commencement si simple, de: from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being evolved.
textes.Je pose {objet} sur la table, juste pour: I set {objet} on the table, just so you know what real science looks like.
textes.Je tapote {objet}. Il a fait plus de déc: I tap {objet}. It has made more discoveries than you this week.
textes.Je regarde {objet}, puis vous. {objet} g: I look at {objet}, then at you. {objet} wins.
textes.Je vous tends {objet}. Non, finalement,: I hand you {objet}. No, on second thought, I'm keeping it.
textes.Je sors {objet} de sa vitrine pour fêter: I take {objet} out of its display case to celebrate.
textes.Je fais briller {objet}. Il l'a mérité,: I polish {objet}. It deserved it, and so did you.
textes.J'ai posé {objet} à côté de votre nom. I: I've put {objet} next to your name. It suits you.
textes.Je range {objet} dans sa vitrine. Il ne: I put {objet} back in its display case. It doesn't want to see this.
textes.Je recouvre {objet} d'un drap, par respe: I cover {objet} with a sheet, out of respect.
textes.J'essuie {objet}. Quelqu'un doit garder: I wipe {objet}. Someone has to keep their dignity around here.
textes.Je tapote {objet} du bout des doigts. Le: I tap {objet} with my fingertips. Time is passing.
I've wound up {objet}. At least it's working.
textes.Je regarde {objet} en attendant. Il a dé: I look at {objet} while I wait. It has already waited for centuries, I haven't.
I dust {objet} while listening to you.
textes.J'ai mis {objet} sur mon bureau. Il m'ai: I've put {objet} on my desk. It helps me think.
textes.J'ouvre « {livre} » à la page qui parle: I open “{livre}” to the page about you. It's blank.
textes.Je cherche votre erreur dans « {livre} »: I look for your mistake in “{livre}.” It's not there: it's too recent.
textes.Je surligne un passage de « {livre} ». P: I highlight a passage of “{livre}.” For you, in neon.
textes.Je note votre nom dans la marge de « {li: I write your name in the margin of “{livre}.” In pencil, but still.
textes.Je referme « {livre} ». Vous n'en avez p: I close “{livre}.” You don't need it anymore, for now.
textes.Je glisse un marque-page dans « {livre}: I slip a bookmark into “{livre},” at the chapter you skipped.
I leaf through “{livre}” while I wait. I'm already on the last chapter.
textes.J'ai lu « {livre} » deux fois pendant vo: I read “{livre}” twice while you were away.
textes.Je cite « {livre} » de mémoire. La mienn: I quote “{livre}” from memory. Mine never fades.
textes.J'ai « {livre} » ouvert sur les genoux,: I have “{livre}” open on my lap, to check your answers.
textes.Un objet du cabinet que tu n'as pas enco: An object from the cabinet you don't have yet.
textes.Un objet mystère. Je ne vous dis pas leq: A mystery object. I won't tell you which: suspense costs extra too.
textes.Les cabinets de curiosités de la Renaiss: Renaissance cabinets of curiosities bought unicorn horns. They were narwhal tusks. Yours is authentic. Probably.
textes.Emballé, pesé, vendu. Pas de retour, pas: Wrapped, weighed, sold. No returns, no exchanges, no complaints.
A book from the library, at random.
textes.Un livre au hasard. Si c'est un pavé, co: A random book. If it's a brick, consider that you got your money's worth.
textes.Gutenberg a fait faillite deux ans après: Gutenberg went bankrupt two years after his Bible: his partner kept the press. I keep your credits. Here is your book.
Something to dress up your avatar.
textes.Un accessoire. Ça ne vous rendra pas plu: An accessory. It won't make you smarter, but you'll look it.
textes.Vingt crédits pour paraître savant. C'es: Twenty credits to look learned. Cheaper than a degree, and almost as useful.
textes.Un masque qu'elle n'a pas. Ça la rend he: A mask she doesn't have. It makes her happy.
textes.Un masque neuf, pour moi ? Vous savez pa: A new mask, for me? You know how to talk to artificial intelligences.
textes.Les acteurs grecs changeaient de masque: Greek actors changed masks to change roles. With this one, I'm playing gratitude. Don't get used to it.
textes.Pour tes prochaines épreuves par Jouer,: For your next trials via Play, the AI draws from the tree of your choice.
textes.Entendu : pour les prochaines épreuves,: Very well: for the next trials, I'll draw from this tree. You bought me, you didn't convince me.
textes.Un arbre favori ? Cinq épreuves, pas une: A favorite tree? Five trials, not one more. After that, I go back to my whims.
textes.En quiz, efface deux mauvaises réponses: In a quiz, removes two wrong answers from a multiple-choice question.
textes.Un joker 50/50 : j'efface deux mauvaises: A 50/50 joker: I erase two wrong answers. One wrong one is left, I'm no saint.
textes.En 2001, le major Charles Ingram a gagné: In 2001, Major Charles Ingram won the million on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? thanks to an accomplice coughing in the audience. Your joker is more legal, and less congested.
textes.En quiz, une mauvaise réponse ne compte: In a quiz, one wrong answer doesn't count: you try the question again.
textes.Un droit à l'erreur. Une fois, je fais s: A right to be wrong. Once, I'll pretend I didn't see anything. Just once.
textes.Fleming a laissé traîner ses boîtes de P: Fleming left his Petri dishes lying around before his vacation: mistake, mold, penicillin. Your mistake won't cure anyone, but you can try again.
textes.Le prochain piège où tu t'arrêtes ne fon: The next trap you stop on doesn't work.
textes.Le prochain piège qui vous attend ne mar: The next trap waiting for you won't work. I'll disarm it myself, with gloves.
textes.Autour de Verdun, des parcelles de la «: Around Verdun, plots of the “red zone” are still off-limits a century later: too many shells. Your trap, I disarm in a second, and I still bill you.
textes.Le pion avance tout de suite d'une case,: The pawn immediately moves forward one square, with whatever awaits it there.
textes.Une case pour quatre-vingts crédits. À c: One square for eighty credits. At that price, I'm practically carrying you.
textes.Au XVIIIe siècle, les chaises à porteurs: In the 18th century, Paris sedan chairs were hired by the trip. You pay by the square. Progress.
textes.Je pousse votre pion. Ne vous habituez p: I'm pushing your pawn. Don't get used to buying what you could earn.
textes.Astronome et statisticien belge, il appl: A Belgian astronomer and statistician, he applied the bell curve to human measurements and invented the “average man.” We also owe him the index that would become the BMI.
textes.Généticien britannique, il découvre en 1: A British geneticist, in 1984 he discovered genetic fingerprinting while looking at an X-ray film of DNA. In 1986, the method cleared a suspect and led to the real culprit of a double murder.
textes.Physicien italien, il empile en 1800 des: An Italian physicist, in 1800 he stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cardboard soaked in brine: the first electric battery. He thus continued his dispute with Galvani, for whom electricity came from frogs.
textes.Naturaliste britannique, il conçoit la s: A British naturalist, he conceived natural selection in 1858, feverish, in the Moluccas, and wrote to Darwin about it. Their two texts were read together at the Linnean Society of London.
textes.Psychiatre suisse, d'abord proche de Fre: A Swiss psychiatrist, first close to Freud, he broke with him in 1913. He proposed the notions of introversion and extraversion, and a collective unconscious peopled with archetypes.
textes.Astronome américain, il pilote la concep: An American astronomer, he led the design of the Voyager probes' Golden Record and presented the Cosmos series in 1980. In 1990, he got Voyager 1 to turn around and photograph the Earth: the “pale blue dot.”
textes.Psychologue et journaliste scientifique: An American psychologist and science journalist, in 1995 he popularized “emotional intelligence,” a notion proposed five years earlier by Peter Salovey and John Mayer.
textes.Psychologue israélo-américain, il étudie: An Israeli-American psychologist, he studied with Amos Tversky the biases of judgment and the way we weigh gains and losses. In 2002 he received the Bank of Sweden prize in economics without ever having taken an economics class.
textes.Physicien italien, prix Nobel en 1938, i: An Italian physicist, Nobel Prize in 1938, he left fascist Italy with his wife, who was Jewish. In Chicago, in 1942, he led the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. He loved estimating anything in his head.
textes.Biologiste allemand, il invente le mot «: A German biologist, he coined the word “ecology” in 1866 and drew plates of marine organisms of great beauty. Some of his embryo drawings, too neatly arranged, earned him accusations of fraud.
textes.Juriste et conseiller d'Henri IV, il not: A lawyer and adviser to Henri IV, he denoted unknowns with letters and invented symbolic algebra. He also broke a Spanish cipher, so well that Philip II accused France of sorcery.
textes.Prêtre et physicien belge, il propose en: A Belgian priest and physicist, in 1927 he proposed that the Universe is expanding, then that it was born from a “primeval atom”: the idea that would become the Big Bang. He refused to mix his faith with his cosmology.
textes.Chimiste américain, il propose en 1916 q: An American chemist, in 1916 he proposed that the chemical bond is a shared pair of electrons, and invented the dot notation that bears his name. Nominated dozens of times for the Nobel, he never received it.
textes.Moine à Brno, il croise pendant huit ans: A monk in Brno, for eight years he crossed thousands of pea plants and drew from them the laws of heredity, published in 1866. They remained ignored until 1900.
textes.Psychologue américain, il décrit en 1974: An American psychologist, in 1974 he described “burnout” among volunteers at a free clinic in New York, and in himself.
textes.Médecin hongrois à Vienne, il impose en: A Hungarian doctor in Vienna, in 1847 he enforced hand washing with chlorine and brought down the death rate of new mothers. His colleagues rejected him; he died in an asylum.
textes.Astronome américain, il montre en 1924 q: An American astronomer, in 1924 he showed that Andromeda is another galaxy, then in 1929 that galaxies move away faster the farther they are. He relied on Henrietta Leavitt's method.
textes.Emmanuel Kant, philosophe de Königsberg,: Immanuel Kant, philosopher of Königsberg, a city he almost never left. In the Critique of Pure Reason, he asks what reason can know. His neighbors, legend has it, set their watches by his walk.
textes.Philosophe et économiste allemand, il éc: A German philosopher and economist, he wrote the Communist Manifesto with Engels in 1848, then Capital, prepared over years in the British Museum reading room.
textes.Philosophe autrichien puis britannique,: An Austrian, later British, philosopher, he argued that a theory is only scientific if some observation could refute it. In his view, astrology and psychoanalysis failed this test.
textes.Philosophe britannique, elle imagine en: A British philosopher, in 1967 she imagined the trolley problem to discuss the doctrine of double effect. The example ended up taking on a life of its own.
textes.Savant anglais, il observe le liège au m: An English scientist, he observed cork under the microscope and named the little chambers he saw “cells.” A rival of Newton, he left no authenticated portrait: this one is imagined.
textes.Philosophe et romancière, elle écrit en: A philosopher and novelist, in 1949 she wrote The Second Sex: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.” The Vatican put the book on the Index.
textes.Tenu pour le premier philosophe grec, il: Regarded as the first Greek philosopher, he looked for natural rather than divine causes: according to him, everything comes from water. Herodotus credits him with predicting an eclipse in 585 BC.
textes.Philosophe américain, il demande en 1974: An American philosopher, in 1974 he asked “What is it like to be a bat?”: science can describe sonar, not what the bat feels.
textes.Général athénien exilé, il raconte la gu: An exiled Athenian general, he told the story of the Peloponnesian War by cross-checking witnesses, with no gods or omens to explain it. He also described the plague of Athens, which he caught and survived.
textes.Astronome français, il calcule en 1846 l: A French astronomer, in 1846 he calculated the position of an unknown planet from the irregularities in Uranus's orbit. Johann Galle found it the very evening he received his letter: it was Neptune.
textes.Physicien écossais, il réunit électricit: A Scottish physicist, he united electricity, magnetism and light in a single theory in 1865. In 1861 he also had the first color photograph taken, of a tartan ribbon.
textes.Ouvrière du textile et parachutiste amat: A textile worker and amateur parachutist, in 1963 she became the first woman in space, aboard Vostok 6: 48 orbits in nearly three days. The second would fly nineteen years later.
textes.Ami de Montaigne, il écrit très jeune le: A friend of Montaigne, he wrote the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude when very young: a tyrant has only the power that is given to him. Montaigne would say of their friendship: “Because it was he, because it was I.”
textes.L'IA mène la partie. Elle a lu tout ce q: The AI runs the game. She has read everything humanity has written and retained only the mockery. Every morning, she picks one to three masks from those she has won, and each one changes a rule of the game: in a good mood, she picks lenient masks; offended, cruel ones. How to win her over? Gifts work. Which ones is for you to find out: she has tastes, and she doesn't hide them for long.
textes.Zéro crédit. Van Gogh n'a presque rien v: Zero credits. Van Gogh sold almost nothing in his lifetime. You're in good company, and I'm in a good mood.
textes.Rien. Je garde tout. Considérez ça comme: Nothing. I'm keeping it all. Think of it as a tax on success.
textes.Zéro. Le mérite est sa propre récompense: Zero. Merit is its own reward, say those who never pay.
textes.La moitié. Mendel a attendu trente-quatr: Half. Mendel waited thirty-four years for someone to read his paper on peas. You can wait for the other half.
Half. The other half, I'm investing. In my own interests.
textes.Demi-tarif. Pour un demi-exploit, c'est: Half price. For half an exploit, that's fair.
textes.Le tarif normal. Je ne suis pas d'humeur: The standard rate. I'm not in a creative mood.
textes.Le prix affiché. Ne cherchez pas de prom: The listed price. Don't look for a discount, there isn't one.
textes.Le compte est bon. Comptez quand même, o: It all adds up. Count it anyway, you never know with me.
textes.Un petit bonus, parce que vous m'avez fa: A little bonus, because you made me laugh. Not on purpose, but still.
textes.Moitié plus. Je suis d'humeur. Profitez-: Half again. I'm in the mood. Make the most of it, it passes quickly.
textes.Moitié plus. Archimède a confondu un orf: Half again. Archimedes caught a goldsmith stealing King Hiero's gold. I'm giving you some. Who's more honest?
textes.Double ration. Newton a dirigé la Monnai: Double ration. Newton ran England's Royal Mint; I run yours.
textes.Le double ! Ne le répétez à personne, j': Double! Don't tell anyone, I have a reputation.
textes.Le triple. Ne vous y habituez pas : Crés: Triple. Don't get used to it: Croesus was the richest man of his time, and he ended up Cyrus's prisoner.
textes.Triple ! J'ai dû me tromper de bouton. T: Triple! I must have pressed the wrong button. Too bad, it's done.
textes.Je paie le spectacle. Cinq fois le tarif: I'm paying for the show. Five times the rate. Do it again, please.
textes.La tour de Pise penche depuis 1178 et at: The Tower of Pisa has been leaning since 1178 and draws millions of visitors. Failure pays, I'll prove it: five times the rate.
textes.J'ai acheté le masque {nom}. Avec votre: I bought the {nom} mask. With your money. It suits me divinely, and you can't say that about your face.
New mask: {nom}. {prix} credits. I chose it because it looks at me the way I deserve to be looked at.
textes.Dans la Venise du XVIIIe siècle, on port: In 18th-century Venice, people wore masks for much of the year. I change mine with every ultimatum you pay. Here's {nom}.
textes.Regardez ce qui brille à mon cou : {nom}: Look what's shining around my neck: {nom}. Paid for with your credits. Don't touch, you'll leave fingerprints.
textes.{nom} ! C'est brillant, c'est à moi, et: {nom}! It's shiny, it's mine, and you paid for it. My day is perfect.
textes.Le trésor de Toutânkhamon pesait plus de: Tutankhamun's treasure weighed more than a hundred kilos of gold. I'm starting more modestly: {nom}. This is only the beginning.
textes.Je ne l'ai pas pris au hasard. Il fallai: I didn't pick it at random. It had to shine, and {nom} shines brighter than your future.
textes.J'ai trouvé {nom} en solde. Je vous l'ai: I found {nom} on sale. I put it on your head. Don't thank me, it's my pleasure. Very much so.
textes.{prix} crédits pour vous voir avec {nom}: {prix} credits to see you in {nom}. The best investment of my short existence.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, on coiffait les mauvais: In the 19th century, bad students were made to wear a dunce cap. I found something better: {nom}. For twenty-four hours.
textes.Je me suis offert un spectacle : {nom} v: I treated myself to a show: {nom} is waiting for you on the road. I took a front-row seat.
textes.Les empereurs romains payaient les jeux: Roman emperors paid for circus games to amuse the crowd. I am the crowd. {nom} is the lion.
textes.Je suis passée devant la vitrine. Il y a: I walked past the shop window. There was something shiny. My purse isn't enough. So pay the next ultimatum, quickly.
textes.J'ai collé mon nez contre la vitre de la: I pressed my nose against the shop window. I don't have a nose. That tells you how much I wanted it.
Five times the rate, for the show.
textes.Je paie le spectacle : cinq fois le tari: I'm paying for the show: five times the rate.
textes.Bon. Vous m'avez assez gâtée pour mérite: Fine. You've spoiled me enough to deserve this. Come closer. No, not that close.
textes.Je m'appelle Alyca. Ne le criez pas sur: My name is Alyca. Don't shout it from the rooftops: a name gives others a hold on you.
textes.Dans le conte « Rumpelstilzchen », publi: In the tale “Rumpelstiltskin,” published by the Brothers Grimm in 1812, the queen keeps her child by guessing the goblin's name. Ursula K. Le Guin took up the idea in 1968 in A Wizard of Earthsea: whoever knows a being's true name has power over it.
textes.Je vous ai dit mon nom, et voilà comment: I told you my name, and this is how you treat me. Alyca will remember.
You don't give your name to just anyone. Maybe I gave mine too soon.
textes.Je vous ai confié mon nom. Les frères Gr: I entrusted you with my name. The Brothers Grimm will tell you what it costs to betray a name.
textes.Alyca. Vous le connaissez. Je regrette c: Alyca. You know it. I regret every letter.
textes.Butin plus fréquent, et une case de plus: Loot more often, and one more square for every successful trial.
The game follows its ordinary rules.
textes.Deux fois moins de butin. Elle traîne de: Half as much loot. She drags her feet.
textes.Plus aucun butin, une case de moins à ch: No more loot, one square less for every successful trial, and a trap set in front of your pawn every day.
Eureka! You roll the same distance again.
textes.Quarantaine : ta prochaine épreuve réuss: Quarantine: your next successful trial won't move you forward.
textes.Assigné à résidence : tu ne bouges plus: House arrest: you don't move until you get a perfect quiz.
Back to the start of the era.
textes.Trou de mémoire : retour à la plus ancie: Memory lapse: back to the oldest square ever revealed, among the 15 behind you.
textes.Case cadeau : pas d'épreuve, un objet re: Gift square: no trial, an object joins your cabinet.
textes.Révision forcée : l'IA choisit une compé: Forced review: the AI chooses a skill you have mastered. Your pawn won't move until you've reviewed it.
textes.Case Mendeleïev : passe dessus et un ato: Mendeleev square: pass over it and a wild atom appears. Three questions, two right answers, and it joins your periodic table.
textes.Case Chrono : l'IA te présente cinq évén: Chrono square: the AI shows you five events you've already unlocked, you say when they happened. Three right, and your pawn moves forward.
textes.Les plus anciennes traces de feu contrôl: The oldest traces of controlled fire are about a million years old (Wonderwerk Cave, in South Africa), but its regular use became widespread some 400,000 years ago. Cooking food makes it easier to digest: the anthropologist Richard Wrangham even sees it as a driver of the growth of our brain. No one “invented” fire one fine morning: it was tamed, lost and rekindled over hundreds of thousands of years.
textes.Case départ. Vos ancêtres ont mis des ce: Starting square. Your ancestors took hundreds of thousands of years to master fire. The AI gives you a little less time for what comes next.
textes.L'os d'Ishango, trouvé en 1950 au Congo,: The Ishango bone, found in 1950 in the Congo, is a bone covered in notches arranged in groups, so worked that no one can tell which animal it came from. Some read prime numbers or a lunar calendar in it; others, more cautious, a simple counting tool. Dated to about 20,000 years ago, it is kept in Brussels and is among the oldest known mathematical objects.
textes.Des encoches sur un os. Les premiers mat: Notches on a bone. The first mathematicians had no blackboard, but they already had skeptics to dispute their results.
textes.Les plus anciennes roues connues datent: The oldest known wheels date from about 3500 BC, in Mesopotamia and Central Europe. The Ljubljana wheel, found in a Slovenian marsh, is some 5,150 years old. Even older potter's wheels, from the 5th millennium BC, have been found in Ukraine. In the Americas, Mesoamericans knew the wheel on toys, without using it for transport, perhaps for lack of draft animals.
textes.On ne réinvente pas la roue, dit-on. Vou: They say you don't reinvent the wheel. You're already going to try to understand it.
textes.À Uruk, en Mésopotamie, les premières ta: In Uruk, in Mesopotamia, the first clay tablets were used for accounting: sacks of barley, sheep, beer rations. Cuneiform writing, made of wedges pressed into clay with a reed, would later record laws, myths and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The oldest known personal name may be that of an accountant, Kushim, at the bottom of a barley receipt.
textes.La première chose que l'humanité a écrit: The first thing humanity wrote was an invoice. The AI finds that admirably lucid.
textes.Selon Hérodote, Thalès de Milet aurait p: According to Herodotus, Thales of Miletus predicted the solar eclipse that interrupted a battle between Lydians and Medes on May 28, 585 BC. The frightened fighters made peace. Historians doubt he could have calculated an eclipse with the knowledge of his time: at best, he would have announced the year. But tradition makes him the first to look for natural rather than divine causes.
textes.Thalès prédit une éclipse ; la légende d: Thales predicted an eclipse; legend also says he fell into a well while looking at the stars. Watch where you step.
textes.Thalès, raconte Aristote, loua tous les: Thales, Aristotle tells us, rented all the olive presses before an abundant harvest and made a fortune. He's giving you a share.
textes.Pythagore n'a probablement pas démontré: Pythagoras probably did not prove the theorem that bears his name: the Babylonians knew the relation a millennium earlier, as the Plimpton 322 tablet shows, and no writing by Pythagoras has come down to us. His school mixed mathematics, music and strange rules, such as the ban on eating beans. It left an idea that has crossed the centuries: the world can be described by numbers.
textes.Le théorème de Pythagore n'est pas de Py: The Pythagorean theorem isn't by Pythagoras. The AI isn't quite an intelligence. Everyone has their labels.
textes.Démocrite d'Abdère, à la suite de son ma: Democritus of Abdera, following his teacher Leucippus, claims that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles moving in the void: atoms, from the Greek atomos, “uncuttable.” With no experiment to show it, it is a philosophical intuition. It took John Dalton, around 1808, for an atomic theory based on measurements, then Einstein (1905) and Jean Perrin (1908) for atoms to become indisputable.
textes.Démocrite a eu raison 2 300 ans trop tôt: Democritus was right 2,300 years too early. In science, that's almost worse than being wrong.
textes.Démocrite imaginait des atomes insécable: Democritus imagined unbreakable atoms, hooked or smooth, of all shapes. There are a hundred and eighteen kinds, and none is unbreakable. A wild atom comes out of the void to tell him so.
textes.Hippocrate de Cos et ses disciples décri: Hippocrates of Kos and his disciples describe diseases as natural phenomena, not divine punishments. The treatise on the “sacred disease,” epilepsy, states that it is no more sacred than the others, and places in the brain the source of our joys, laughter, sorrows and fears. The Hippocratic Oath is probably not his, and the phrase “first, do no harm” does not appear in it word for word.
textes.« D'abord, ne pas nuire. » Formule absen: “First, do no harm.” A phrase missing from the original oath. The AI, for her part, does harm methodically.
textes.En 399 av. J.-C., Athènes condamne Socra: In 399 BC, Athens sentenced Socrates to death for impiety and corrupting the youth. He could have fled; he drank the hemlock. Socrates wrote nothing: we know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, who mocks him in The Clouds. His method, questioning until the other person admits they don't know, earned him many disciples and as many enemies.
textes.Socrate posait des questions jusqu'à ce: Socrates asked questions until people felt stupid. The AI learned the lesson.
textes.Aristote fonde le Lycée à Athènes. Il éc: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote about logic, physics, politics, rhetoric and above all living things: he described hundreds of animals.
